lesson.title: Shrink or Swell: How Forming an Ion Changes an Atom's Size
lesson.summary: Losing electrons to form a cation shrinks an atom dramatically, while gaining electrons to form an anion swells it, and comparing radii across an isoelectronic series shows nuclear charge alone deciding the winner.
lesson.body:
Ionic radius is the natural extension of atomic radius to charged particles, measured the same operational way, typically from the distances between ions packed together in a crystal lattice, such as table salt. Two simple rules govern the comparison between an atom and the ion it forms. A cation, a positive ion formed by losing one or more electrons, is always smaller than its neutral parent atom. An anion, a negative ion formed by gaining one or more electrons, is always larger than its neutral parent atom.

Both effects come straight out of the effective nuclear charge logic from the periodic trends chapter, just applied to a change in electron count rather than a change in position on the table. When an atom loses its valence electrons to form a cation, it often loses its entire outermost shell at once, since many atoms only had one, two, or three electrons up there to begin with; the new outermost shell sits one full principal level closer to the nucleus, and the same nuclear charge now pulls on fewer electrons, raising the effective nuclear charge each remaining electron feels. When an atom gains extra electrons to form an anion, those electrons crowd into the same outer shell that was already there, increasing electron-electron repulsion among a fixed number of protons and effectively lowering the nuclear pull each electron feels, so the whole electron cloud spreads outward.

The size change can be dramatic. Sodium has an atomic radius of about 186 pm. Once it loses its lone 3s valence electron to form Na+, the remaining electrons are the 1s2 2s2 2p6 configuration, identical in electron count and shell structure to neon, and the ionic radius drops all the way to about 102 pm, nearly cut in half, precisely because an entire principal shell disappeared. Chlorine runs the opposite direction: its atomic radius of about 99 pm swells to about 181 pm as Cl-, once it gains one more electron to complete a stable 3p6 octet, since that extra electron adds repulsion within the same outer shell without any new proton to compensate.

The cleanest demonstration of pure effective nuclear charge comes from an isoelectronic series, a set of ions that all share the exact same number of electrons, 10 in this case, matching neon's 1s2 2s2 2p6 configuration: O2-, F-, Na+, Mg2+, and Al3+. Since every species in this series has identical electron count and identical shielding, the only variable left is nuclear charge, and the radii track it perfectly: O2- (Z = 8) is about 140 pm, F- (Z = 9) is about 133 pm, Na+ (Z = 11) is about 102 pm, Mg2+ (Z = 12) is about 72 pm, and Al3+ (Z = 13) is about 53.5 pm. As nuclear charge climbs while electron count stays fixed at 10, the same ten electrons get reeled in progressively tighter, and the radius shrinks steadily and predictably.

Ionic radius is not just a number for comparing sizes: it governs how tightly oppositely charged ions pack together in a crystal, which affects a compound's lattice energy, solubility, and melting point, topics that build directly on the geometry established here. Taken together, atomic radius and ionic radius show the same effective nuclear charge mechanism playing out in two different settings, across the periodic table and across a change in electron count, and that single mechanism will keep reappearing whenever new periodic properties get introduced.
